notes: Route evidence is contested across practitioner sources; see verification issue V-002.

aliases.notes: Not a synonym. Analytical characterisation of the TB-500 formulation identifies it as Ac-LKKTETQ, the N-terminally acetylated 17-23 fragment of this peptide: seven residues of forty-three, about one fifth of the mass. Practitioner sources and some 2026 peer-reviewed papers use the two names interchangeably; this index does not, and keeps a separate record for the fragment. Verification issue V-001, resolved 13 September 2026 by SRC-041 and SRC-042 and left open on the separate question of what any given product contains (SRC-043).

notes: Has genuine human trial evidence, which is unusual in this register and is attached to the full-length peptide rather than to the name practitioners use.

aliases.notes: Practitioner name for this albumin-binding molecule; DAC (drug affinity complex) was the developer's term for the technology.
The 29-residue core peptide without the albumin-binding lysine. A different molecule with its own record.

notes: The albumin-binding GHRH analogue the originator defined (tetrasubstituted hGRF(1-29) plus a maleimidopropionamide lysine). Products and handbooks also use the name for modified GRF (1-29), which has its own record; evidence must not cross between the two.

aliases.notes: The usual market and handbook name, and misleading: CJC-1295 in the scientific literature is the albumin-binding molecule, which has its own record. Recorded as a misnomer so search surfaces the confusion.

notes: Kept as a record of its own because the originator's CJC-1295 is a different molecule, and a product sold as CJC-1295 was analysed and found to be this 29-residue peptide. Evidence must not cross between the two.

aliases.notes: Transliteration of the Russian name used in some journal titles.
A chemically modified form sold as a nootropic; not the registered heptapeptide, and not the molecule the human studies used.
Earlier designation used in the 1990s literature.

notes: Investigational. Development status is time-sensitive and must be re-checked before any publication. Verification issue V-003.

aliases.notes: The sequence the analytical literature identifies in the TB-500 formulation.
Sold alongside TB-500 and analysed with it in SRC-043, which found product contents inconsistent with their descriptions. No source held here establishes what TB1000 is.

Widely used for this substance and incorrect: thymosin beta-4 is the full 43-residue peptide, of which this is residues 17-23. Recorded as a misnomer rather than a synonym so that search surfaces the confusion instead of resolving it.

notes: Kept as a record of its own because the evidence says it is a different molecule from Thymosin beta-4. Evidence must not cross between the two.
The only compound in the Section 4 expansion with held literature of its own (SRC-153, SRC-154). Clinical use is described by a practitioner handbook only.

A practitioner handbook reports that a product containing this peptide is FDA-approved for one narrow indication. No regulator's record has been consulted; the approval is recorded as reported, not verified.

The handbook lists Epithalamin as another name, but the mortality trials it reports under that name concern a pineal extract rather than this tetrapeptide. Kept related-but-distinct so findings do not transfer silently.
Unsubstituted GHRH(1-29). Kept separate from the mod-grf-1-29 record, which is the tetrasubstituted analogue of the same fragment; no evidence crosses between them.
The handbook's rare-adverse-reaction list for this compound is identical to the one it prints for kisspeptin; recorded on both records as boilerplate.
A different molecule from thymosin-beta-4 and tb-500 despite the shared family name. No evidence crosses between the three records.

The source describes kisspeptin as a family formed by differential proteolysis and does not say which member its regimen refers to. No alias created for kisspeptin-10, which the handbook does not mention.
The monograph's intranasal titration chart is too poorly rendered in the held copy to transcribe; only the start, strength change and final dose are recorded.
Class C by decision: comparator mentions inside retatrutide literature are not dedicated semaglutide evidence and were not used to promote this record.

One held source spells the name three ways on facing pages. 'AOD-9604 + HA' is the handbook's name for the hyaluronic acid combination, recorded as related but distinct because it is a combination rather than a different molecule. The printed sequence lists twelve residues while the summary describes a hexadecapeptide fragment; the conflict is recorded rather than resolved.

Three names in one source: ARA-290, cibinetide acetate and Helix B surface peptide. The alias is recorded as the source gives it, including the salt form; no bare 'cibinetide' alias was invented, and a search for cibinetide matches the recorded alias anyway.

The three N-terminal residues of alpha-MSH. Alpha-MSH is recorded as related but distinct, never a synonym: the same source states KPV does not bind the melanocortin receptors alpha-MSH acts through. The handbook's category label calls KPV an alpha-MSH stimulating peptide, which its own text does not support.

Nonathymulin is a synonym: the source lists it and uses it for the peptide studied in the trials it reports. Thymalin is recorded as related but distinct, because the source asserts the identity and nothing held supports it. The 'Thyamlin' row in SRC-004 has not been attached to this record at all — the spelling is closer to Thymalin, and the indication differs. The printed molecular weight is inconsistent with the printed nine-residue sequence and is not carried on the identity record.

One record for MGF with PEG-MGF recorded as related but distinct: the source covers them in one monograph and describes PEG-MGF as the same peptide pegylated to extend its half-life from minutes to days, so it is a preparation with its own regimen rather than a separate molecule. IGF-1 LR3 appears in the regimens as a pairing and is deliberately not an alias.

PNC-28 is a different peptide, six residues shorter, and is recorded as related but distinct because the handbook reports much of its cell-line evidence for both together. No category fits an anticancer peptide in the current taxonomy, so it is uncategorised rather than forced into one. The printed dosage is not physically possible and is recorded with that stated inline rather than transcribed as usable.

Larazotide acetate is the name the source uses for the studied material and is recorded as a synonym. The abbreviation 'LA' used inside the monograph is deliberately not an alias: two letters colliding with ordinary text are worse than useless in a search index. No research code or brand name was added, because the source gives none.
